planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; Brantwood is an RHS Award of Garden Merit selection of giant bellflower grown for flower color noticeably deeper than the species.

directions: Set divisions into moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade, where Brantwood sends up sturdy upright stems lined with large, nettle-like leaves through early summer. Its tubular, outward-facing bells open in a rich, saturated violet-purple noticeably darker than the species, lining the upper third of each stem from June into July and drawing bumblebees readily. It holds up well in deep shade where few other tall-flowering perennials bloom with equal vigor, pairing naturally with hostas and ferns at the back of a woodland border. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the clump and divide only when flowering declines, since established crowns resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Flavomaculata Japanese Bamboo Fern (Yellow-Banded Variegated Coniogramme)

planting.note: Divide established rhizomatous clumps in spring or plant container stock in moist, humus-rich soil in light to partial shade; Flavomaculata is an RHS-recognized variegated selection of Japanese bamboo fern grown for its herringbone-patterned leaflet markings.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in light to partial shade, sheltered from drying wind. Flavomaculata carries the same broad, undivided, bamboo-like leaflets as the straight species, but each one is overlaid with small irregular yellow markings arranged in a herringbone pattern along the pinnae, an effect most vivid on new spring growth before mellowing as the fronds mature. The slowly spreading rhizomes build a graceful colony over several seasons, and the variegated texture reads as a bright accent against plain-green hostas and darker ferns nearby. Protect the crown with a loose mulch at the cold end of its range, since hard freezes can damage emerging fronds before they harden off.

common_name: Brilliantelse Maidenhair Fern (Pink-Flushed New Growth Adiantum)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Brilliantelse is an RHS Award of Garden Merit maidenhair selection prized for its denser habit and colorful emerging fronds.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade with steady humidity, keeping the fine root system from ever drying fully. New fronds emerge in soft pink to violet tones before settling to the typical bright green of the species, giving the clump a two-toned seasonal look as fresh growth continually replaces older fronds. Its habit is noticeably denser and more compact than the common delta maidenhair, making it a tidy choice for small pots, terrariums, and shaded windowsills rather than hanging baskets. Mist regularly and shield from drafts and heating vents, since dry air browns the delicate pinnae quickly.

common_name: Fragrant Blue Hosta (Paul Aden Gardenia-Scented Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Fragrant Blue is a Paul Aden introduction and the parent of several later sports, including the cream-edged sport Blue Flame.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade, where consistent moisture keeps the thick chalky-blue leaves from fading toward green. Fragrant Blue builds into a large, vigorous mound of heart-shaped, rippled foliage within a couple of seasons, and in midsummer sends up scapes carrying pale lavender flowers with a distinct gardenia-like fragrance that carries well beyond the plant itself. It has proven a useful breeding parent, having produced variegated sports prized for combining its blue leaf color with contrasting margins. Site it where afternoon sun cannot reach it, since direct light both scorches the leaves and accelerates the loss of the blue, waxy bloom.

common_name: Bunny Blue Sedge (Hobb Silvery-Blue Spreading Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in medium to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Hobb, sold under the trade name Bunny Blue, is a Head Brothers Nursery selection valued for foliage noticeably bluer than the wild species.

directions: Plant in humus-rich soil that stays medium to wet in partial to full shade, where Hobb forms a dense, rounded clump of arching, glaucous silvery-blue leaves that hold their color far more consistently than the plain green of wild spreading sedge. Inconspicuous flower spikes appear in spring but add little to its appeal, since the fine-textured blue foliage carries the display through the whole growing season. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes into a slowly widening patch, making it useful as a matrix groundcover beneath deciduous trees or paired with hostas and ferns for color contrast. Evergreen in most winters; shear old foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth resumes.
